cards.title: Turn Personal Interests Into Amazon Product Ideas
cards.summary: Mine your own interests, hobbies and daily frustrations, then validate them as Amazon search demand instead of guessing at random products.
cards.use_when: You're starting product selection for an Amazon FBA store and have no candidate products yet.
steps: List your interests, daily rituals and annoyances (shower, a sport you're learning, a diet you follow, a hobby). Each line is a possible niche.
For each interest, list product ideas that would serve someone with the same interest — the source generated tea, meditation cushions, flashcards, electrolyte powder from this exercise.

Take one interest and plug it into a keyword tool (the source used Helium 10 Magnet), set title density filter to 0 to bias toward low-competition phrases, sort by the tool's opportunity/IQ score, and read the list one by one.

Flag any search phrase where the results are poorly branded or where the exact phrase isn't in competitors' titles — e.g. 'baby dish soap' had ~10,000 monthly searches but the leading listing didn't even use the phrase in its title.
Repeat for other interests, and log every idea found so far in one running list; most will be rejected later.
Rebuild your own version of the product better (branding, vegan/carbon-neutral positioning, name matching the keyword) rather than copying an existing listing.
caveats: The source's revenue figures (e.g. an $11k/month chicken-flour listing, a soap bar at ~$900k/month) are individual examples, not benchmarks.
Keyword tool interfaces and scores change; verify current UI and that a filter still exists before relying on it.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Systematically Narrow Amazon's Category Tree to a Niche
cards.summary: Use Amazon's Best Sellers category tree with an interest rating to cut 20,000+ subcategories down to a shortlist worth researching.
cards.use_when: You're doing broad product selection and want a repeatable way to screen Amazon categories instead of browsing aimlessly.
steps: Go to amazon.com, open the Best Sellers tab, and use the category sidebar to drill into subcategories of subcategories; there are over 20,000.
Uncheck every top-level category you would not want to sell in (the source eliminated appliances, automotive, baby, books, electronics, clothing, industrial, etc.).
Work down level by level, unchecking subcategories you have no interest in, until the list is manageable.
For remaining subcategories, write a 1–5 interest score (leave blank if not interested) plus short notes on why.
For any subcategory that scores highly, open its Best Sellers list and look at how much the top products appear to earn and how strong their branding is.
Look for a product that is niched down within that subcategory (the source used a Dr. Squatch men's soap gift set as an example of a narrowly-targeted winner).
Open a top competitor's product page, copy its ASIN, and run it through a reverse-ASIN keyword tool (the source used Helium 10 Cerebro, title density 0) to see the exact search phrases buyers use.
Filter out phrases containing brand names, then evaluate the low-competition phrases that remain as product angles.
caveats: Interest is a filter, not validation — the source explicitly says not every idea on the list will be a winner.
Relying on visible sales estimates is approximate; verify with your own numbers before committing.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Mine Credit Card, Amazon Browse and Google History for Product Ideas
cards.summary: Your own spending and search history reveal categories where you'd be a credible, motivated seller.
cards.use_when: Product selection is stalled and you can't name a product you'd be excited to build.
steps: Download your credit card history and find categories where you personally spend more than average — the source spotted heavy spending on studio/content gear and started brainstorming creator products.

Review your Amazon browse history and note products you'd buy if you had more money; the source's first product, a premium nut butter at ~$28/box, sold to people willing to pay more than he would have.
Check your Google history and podcast subscriptions for recurring interests that map to product categories.
Convert findings into concrete product briefs (e.g. a camera that films horizontally and vertically at once) rather than vague categories.
Cross-check each idea against Amazon search demand and competition before spending money.
caveats: This generates candidates only; popularity with you is not evidence of demand.
Spend-based hobbies can still be small markets — validate with keyword volume.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Why Cheap Products Fail and the $15–$85 Price Band
cards.summary: The source's core price filter: cheap, low-barrier products invite price wars and PPC losses, while the $15–$85 band supports impulse purchase and margin.
cards.use_when: You're choosing a selling price or screening a product candidate on price before ordering inventory.
steps: Reject products priced under roughly $15: the source argues Amazon fees make them unprofitable and the low barrier draws thousands of new sellers into price wars.
Reject products over roughly $85: the source argues Amazon buyers move from product view to checkout in under three minutes on average, so higher prices force research and reduce impulse conversion.
Target the $15–$85 band, which the source states he has used across 10 years of selling and teaching over 1,000 FBA sellers.
Model a worked example: on a $30 sale, budget about $10 product cost, about $10 Amazon fees, and about $10 profit — roughly a 30% margin.
Keep the 30% margin as a floor and seek higher where possible; adjust for size and weight, which change Amazon fees.
Note the PPC math that kills cheap products: at $1 per click on a $10 item, a few clicks erase the entire profit.
caveats: The $15–$85 band and 30% margin are the source's heuristics, not calculated rules; his own reasoning is based on typical fee structures and observed impulse behavior.
4,000 new sellers joining Amazon daily is the source's stated figure — treat as context, not a precise forecast.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Screen Out Trend, Seasonal and Restricted Products
cards.summary: Avoid product categories whose demand window or compliance burden makes inventory risky for a new FBA seller.
cards.use_when: You're shortlisting products and need to disqualify unsuitable categories before ordering.
steps: Cut trend products (fidget spinners and similar): the source says the window is often a week, while manufacturing plus shipping to Amazon takes about two months, leaving you with unsellable units and long-term storage fees.
Cut seasonal products (holiday decorations, Valentine's items): demand is annual only, forcing a guess on yearly inventory and triggering Amazon long-term storage fees after about six months.

Cut restricted and prohibited categories unless you're prepared for approval costs: the source lists alcohol, adult products, dangerous goods, lithium batteries and anything containing them, tobacco, medication, and CBD (he reports sellers in CBD getting banned).
Before finalizing, check Amazon's current restricted-products list yourself for your chosen category.
Instead of a trend, look for evergreen searches where demand persists year-round.
caveats: Restricted-product rules change and vary by category — verify current policy before relying on this list.
Some seasonal products can work as a secondary line if you manage inventory tightly; the source frames this as a rule he follows, not a universal law.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Find Product Gaps by Reading Competitor Reviews and Size Ranges
cards.summary: Use the 'hole in the market' method: identify a missing size, variant or fix from competitor reviews and existing listings.
cards.use_when: You're choosing a product to improve rather than invent, and want a defensible point of difference.
steps: Scan existing listings in a niche for gaps in size or variant — the source's student Brent noticed a large and small blowtorch but no medium, built one, and the source reports over $1M in sales the following year.
Read the negative and mixed reviews on competing listings and record recurring complaints (too big, too small, wrong color, missing option).
Look for colors or configurations people ask for that aren't currently sold on Amazon.
Design your product to directly answer the most common complaint, then state that fix clearly in the listing copy, title and images.
Confirm the gap has search demand before committing, since an unfilled gap may simply mean no demand.
caveats: Brent's $1M result is one example under particular conditions, not a guaranteed outcome.
The complaint you fix must be a purchase driver, not a minor gripe.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Verify a Niche Isn't Brand-Dominated Before Entering
cards.summary: Check whether a dominant brand already owns the category before you try to compete there.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating a product category and deciding whether a new seller can realistically win listings.
steps: Search the category and identify whether a small set of major brands controls it — the source uses shoes (Nike, Adidas, Sketchers, Crocs) as an example he would not enter.
If brands dominate, pick a narrower niche where no single brand owns the search results, so you can build your own brand position.
Check the reverse-ASIN keywords for the category and confirm buyers use generic phrases rather than brand-name phrases, since brand searches route to the incumbent.
Combine this with the price-disparity check: if competitors cluster at nearly identical prices (e.g. floss picks spanning about $2–$16), buyers default to the cheapest and you have no pricing room.
Prefer markets where versions sell at very different prices ($5 vs $95 in the source's illustration), which shows customers aren't buying on price alone.
caveats: This is a screening heuristic, not a market-share calculation; you'd need real share data to quantify dominance.
The $5/$95 spread is an illustrative example, not a researched threshold.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Pack Titles With the Exact Phrases Buyers Search
cards.summary: Amazon is a purchase-intent search engine; naming and titling your product with real search phrases puts you in front of buyers who want that exact thing.
cards.use_when: You're writing your product title and back-end keywords, or deciding whether a product idea has enough keyword surface to work.
steps: Accept that listings win by matching search phrasing: the source named his product 'Carnivore Electrolytes' because searches for 'carnivore electrolytes' had demand and no matching product existed.
Pull the keyword set for your niche from a keyword tool, filter to title density 0 or low competition, and sort by opportunity score.

Build a title that leads with the highest-demand phrase and packs secondary phrases — the source's example title strings together carnivore electrolytes, premium hydration powder, zero carb, keto friendly, energy and recovery, 90 servings.
Prefer products describable by many phrases (an iPhone case can be slim, black, drop-resistant, waterproof, for workmen, for small hands) because more phrases mean more entry points.
Avoid products with only one or two descriptive phrases — the source warns a single keyphrase (his 'yellow umbrella' example) lets competitors undercut and cut you off.
caveats: Keyword volumes and competition shift; re-validate before launch.
The source notes his own example title could likely be improved.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Confirm Demand and Value Before You Commit Inventory
cards.summary: Two baseline checks the source says new sellers skip: there must be real demand, and the product must solve a problem worth paying for.
cards.use_when: You're about to commit to a product and need a go/no-go check before sampling and manufacturing.
steps: Confirm high demand and low competition together — the source says missing either one kills profitability, and warns not to skimp on research.
Check that the product solves a real problem; 'dollars follow value' — the more value delivered, the more sales and five-star reviews accumulate.
Validate before spending on tooling or bulk inventory — the source cites a student, Edgar, losing around $10,000 after launching with non-premium packaging due to incomplete research.

Confirm the product is something you're genuinely interested in; the source ties his own turnaround (over $10,000/month profit within two months of launching a passion product) to selling something he believed in.
Decide whether the product would make a good gift, which the source keeps in mind because Q4 (October–December) concentrates e-commerce spending and gift-friendly products ride that wave.
caveats: Edgar's $10,000 loss and the source's own sales are individual examples, not guarantees.
'Passion' is motivational in the source's framing; it does not substitute for demand and margin validation.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Model Amazon Fees, Landed Cost and Budget Before Choosing
cards.summary: Know your numbers early — manufacturing, freight, Amazon fees and your cash runway — because the product choice is constrained by the math.
cards.use_when: You're deciding between product candidates and need to know what each one will cost you to launch.
steps: List the fee components that scale with your product: pick-and-pack, selling fee, storage, receiving fees; these vary with size and weight.
Calculate landed cost: manufacture plus freight into the destination country.
Set an explicit launch budget before selling so you can sustain the business through the first inventory cycle, not just the sample.
Run each candidate product through a fee calculator rather than estimating by hand.
Keep spending as low as possible at launch, and consider more expensive products only after the business is established.
Use the 30% margin target as the output check: cost, fees and profit should each be roughly a third of a $30 sale.
caveats: Fee structures change; verify current Amazon fee schedules.
The source recommends low initial spend but his own example, student AJ, spent over $20,000 to launch — costs vary widely by product.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Make a Free Physical Prototype From a Manufacturer's Sample
cards.summary: Get to a physical mockup cheaply by mocking up with stationery first, then requesting a free blank sample from a manufacturer.
cards.use_when: You've picked a product and need to see and feel it before paying for tooling or design.
steps: Prototype the format for free with materials at hand — the source's student AJ wrote card designs with Sharpies on blank flashcards until a layout looked right.
Search Alibaba for manufacturers already making similar products (e.g. flashcards, paper goods) and message them with approximate dimensions and specs.
Ask for a sample; the source reports manufacturers often send a blank or leftover sample from a prior project and you only pay shipping (about $50 in his example).
Use the sample to confirm dimensions and physical quality before moving to design.
Then commission a designer to produce a logo, box design and a few sample cards, print the artwork yourself and glue it onto the manufacturer's sample box to create your first realistic prototype.
When you can't pay a designer upfront, request sample work first and agree a small deposit.
caveats: Free samples depend on the manufacturer and are not guaranteed.
A blank sample confirms form factor, not final print quality or material durability — verify those with a printed sample later.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Crowdfund Your Launch Instead of Self-Funding Inventory
cards.summary: Use pre-orders on a crowdfunding platform plus social content to fund design, manufacturing and freight.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product and prototype but limited cash for design, tooling and inventory.
steps: Build the prototype first (physical sample plus designed artwork on the box) so backers can see a real thing.
Set a funding goal tied to your next specific cost — the source's student AJ set a $1,500 goal to cover the designer's down payment.
Produce content in your niche (AJ made cocktail videos on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram) to funnel viewers to the campaign.
Run the campaign for an initial amount and continue past the goal; AJ raised over $1,500 initially and finished near $4,500, covering a $3,600 design bill.

Print a sample of the finished product, then post a story-driven video about your journey and show the finished sample — AJ's TikTok got over 600,000 views and pushed the campaign above $37,000, about $22,000 in one day.
Use raised funds for manufacturing (about $9,000 for 1,500 units in this case) and shipping, so you put in zero of your own dollars.
caveats: This is one student's result; virality is not repeatable or predictable.
Backers expect delivery, so timelines and quality commitments carry real risk.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Choose Air vs Sea Freight for First Inventory
cards.summary: Trade freight cost against speed when shipping first inventory from overseas, especially against pre-order promises.
cards.use_when: You're arranging inbound shipment for your first or reorder inventory and deciding air vs sea.
steps: Compare the two modes: air arrives in roughly 5–7 days but costs substantially more; sea runs about $2 per kilogram but takes six weeks minimum (figures from the source's own experience).
Weigh urgency against margin: air is expensive enough that the source calls it throwing money down the drain unless you really need the speed.
Split the shipment if you only need partial urgency — AJ shipped half air and half sea, paying around $4,200 for the air portion.
If you took crowdfunding pre-orders, factor your delivery promise into the decision, since backers expect the product quickly.
Confirm current rates and transit times before booking; freight pricing fluctuates.
caveats: The per-kg and transit figures are anecdotal from the source's shipments, not current market rates.
Air freight raises landed cost, which reduces the margin cushion you validated earlier.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Use a Premium Brand and Packaging to Justify a Higher Price
cards.summary: Branding lets two identically-priced-to-make products sell at very different prices, changing profit per sale.
cards.use_when: You're setting your listing price and designing packaging, logo and brand identity for a new product.
steps: Treat brand as a pricing lever: the source shows two products with the same manufacturing cost where the branded one sells for double — which he says yields roughly triple the profit per sale.
Prioritize the logo first, since the source argues it sets the tone for packaging, social media and everything else in the brand system.
Write a clear design brief: what the product/brand is, who it's for, desired feel, and required colors.

Choose a sourcing route by budget: Fiverr and Upwork can work if you review many portfolios first (the source's $10 Fiverr pick was unusable, a $50 Upwork logo was usable but not right); 99 Designs crowdsources multiple designers with tiers roughly $300–$1,300, and he used it for a prior successful product.
If using 99 Designs, run the two-round contest, shortlist six finalists, tell them which concept to beat, then have your community vote on the shortlist.
Test the resulting design with your audience before finalizing — the source's community rejected several otherwise-professional drafts.
caveats: The double-price/triple-profit example is illustrative; results depend on category and buyer.
Logo and designer prices are the source's observed ranges and may differ now; verify current platform pricing and interfaces.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Hire Low-Cost Design and Support Help From OnlineJobs.ph
cards.summary: Staff ongoing design, editing, social and customer-service work with full-time overseas hires at low hourly rates.
cards.use_when: You're running an Amazon brand and need recurring creative or support labor without agency costs.
steps: Use the source's preferred platform, onlinejobs.ph, to find full-time hires at roughly $3–$5 per hour.
Deploy hires on repeatable tasks: the source used a full-time graphic designer for thumbnails and video edits, plus people for social media, FAQ/email responses and customer service.
Keep your own time for the work you're best at (product, brand, content), and delegate the rest.
Ask for sample work and start with a small deposit-based trial before committing to a full workload.
caveats: Rates and platform practices are from the source's experience and may differ now; verify current pricing.
Task descriptions, review processes and communication standards still need to be set by you.
